title: Optimal universal approximation factor for EFX
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal:
Determine the universal additive-goods EFX approximation constant
\[\alpha_* = \sup\{\alpha\in[0,1]:\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall m\ge0\ \forall v\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times m}\ \exists A\in\mathcal A_{n,m},\ A\text{ is }\alpha\text{-EFX for }v\}.\]
Here \(n,m\) are integers, \(\mathcal A_{n,m}\) is the set of complete allocations of \(m\) goods to \(n\) agents, and \(\alpha\)-EFX uses the positive-good convention defined below. The requested benchmark precision is absolute error at most \(1/100\): supply a real number \(a\) and prove \(|a-\alpha_*|\le1/100\). This is an existence constant with unrestricted allocation computation, not a polynomial-time approximation threshold.
why: This constant measures how much of the demanding EFX fairness comparison can always be guaranteed when all indivisible goods must be assigned. It gives a quantitative target even if exact EFX existence is unresolved. Its scope is every number of agents and every additive valuation profile, so improvements for special structures do not alone determine the universal guarantee.
status_note: The source survey v2, Amanatidis–Markakis–Ntokos v2 Theorem 4.4, the frontier paper v3 dated 29 July 2026, and Filos-Ratsikas–Kalantzis–Wang v1 Section 1.1 and Definition 2.1 were read on 2026-09-14. The checked recent work retains a distinction between unrestricted additive EFX, restricted agent classes, and removal of multiple goods. A bounded search through this date found no determination of the universal constant to the requested tolerance or exact all-agent additive EFX resolution. The source-open status is limited by this literature check, and does not assert independent verification of the cited algorithmic proofs.

progress.text: A universal \((\sqrt5-1)/2\)-EFX guarantee is established for additive goods.
The source survey asks for the best universal existence factor in Open Problem 3.
The frontier paper obtains \(2/3\)-EFX for several restricted instance families.
A preprint gives \(2/3\)-EFX for eight agents and separate all-agent guarantees when more than one good may be removed.
The revised frontier paper continues to distinguish the general golden-ratio guarantee from stronger restricted results.

sentences: The target is the best multiplicative EFX fairness factor that every finite additive-goods instance admits.
Every good must be allocated, and the comparison removes any good that the potentially envious agent values positively.
There is no bound on the number of agents and no computational-time restriction on choosing the allocation.
Known universal guarantees reach the golden-ratio factor, while stronger results impose instance restrictions or allow removal of more goods.
The benchmark asks for a Lean-certified numerical answer within one hundredth, which need not decide exact EFX existence.

definitions:
Write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) for integers \(k\ge0\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). Each entry \(v_{ig}\) is a finite nonnegative real number giving agent \(i\)'s value for good \(g\). For a bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\), its value is \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\). No normalization, strict positivity, integrality, rationality, number-of-types or agreement-on-ordering assumption is imposed on values.

A complete allocation \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) is an ordered partition of \([m]\): the bundles are pairwise disjoint and their union is all of \([m]\). Empty bundles are allowed. There are no payments, negative-valued chores, fractional goods, discarded goods or additional efficiency constraints.

For \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), the allocation is \(\alpha\)-EFX if
\[\forall i,j\in[n]\ \forall g\in A_j:\quad v_{ig}>0\ \Longrightarrow\ v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha\,v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\}).\]
Both the test of whether the removed good has positive value and the bundle comparison use the potentially envious agent \(i\)'s values. If every good of \(A_j\) has value zero to \(i\), there is no constraint for that pair. If the remaining bundle has value zero, the inequality is automatically satisfied. This is Definition 6 of the source survey. The stronger per-allocation convention often called EFX-zero tests also removed goods of zero value; the card does not silently substitute that convention.

The universally feasible set in the supremum is nonempty, because it includes zero, and is bounded above by one by definition. The constant is dimensionless. Its quantifier order allows a different allocation for each valuation matrix; no single common partition must serve all profiles. Neither an efficient algorithm nor any oracle-access restriction is part of the existence guarantee.

For a fixed finite instance \(v\), one can equivalently define \(\beta(v)\) as the largest \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) for which some complete allocation is \(\alpha\)-EFX. This maximum exists: there are finitely many allocations, and each has a closed interval of feasible factors. Then \(\alpha_*\) is the infimum of these \(\beta(v)\) over all permitted instance sizes and profiles. There need not be one instance attaining this infimum. This equivalent definition makes the universal lower-bound and worst-instance upper-bound meanings explicit.

Exact equality \(\alpha_*=1\) is equivalent to existence of a complete EFX allocation for every additive instance: for each fixed instance, finitely many allocations and closed inequalities prevent loss of the endpoint. A numerical answer within \(1/100\) need not decide that exact equality. The present acceptance tolerance measures the numerical constant and does not relax the definition of \(\alpha\)-EFX itself.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number \(a\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|a-\alpha_*|\le1/100\). A certified interval of width at most \(1/50\) containing \(\alpha_*\) qualifies via its midpoint; an exact value also qualifies. Bounds must concern all finite nonnegative additive instances and complete allocations under the stated positive-good convention. A universal construction proves only a lower bound on the constant unless accompanied by sufficient upper information. An upper bound may be established without a worst instance attaining the infimum. Restricted numbers of agents, partial allocations, nonadditive counterexamples, or guarantees allowing removal of multiple goods do not by themselves determine this constant. A simulation or an unproved decimal estimate is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 3 asks for the best factor guaranteeing existence. The survey separately asks about efficient computation, and this card retains the existence interpretation. The related exact EFX card asks whether the endpoint one is universally attainable.

Amanatidis, Markakis and Ntokos prove a universal factor \((\sqrt5-1)/2\), approximately \(0.618\), in Theorem 4.4. Their definition tests every removed good, including zero-valued goods, so their guarantee also implies the positive-good condition here. This supplies a lower bound on \(\alpha_*\), not its proved optimal value.

The EC 2024 work establishes \(2/3\)-EFX under restrictions including at most seven agents or at most three common value levels. Its July 2026 revision still identifies the golden-ratio bound as the general all-agent additive guarantee. Those restricted \(2/3\) theorems do not establish \(\alpha_*\ge2/3\).

The May 2026 paper extends the \(2/3\)-EFX guarantee to eight agents. It also gives all-agent results for EFkX with \(k\ge2\), where the comparison permits removing a set of \(k\) goods; it expressly states that this general theorem does not apply when \(k=1\). These are distinct from the universal single-good constant.
The numerical tolerance belongs to benchmark acceptance. It allows a certified approximation of the constant without claiming that the exact EFX existence question has been decided.
